title: Show HN: Official MCP Servers
content:
The curated directory of official MCP servers.
No unofficial forks, no abandoned projects, just servers you can trust.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets AI assistants connect to external tools and data. An MCP server exposes what a product can do (query a database, create a ticket, send an email), and any MCP client such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor can use it.
An MCP server can read your data and act on your behalf, so who built it matters. Every entry here is an official server from the company behind the product, or a widely used open source project. Where there is no public repository, we link the vendor's official MCP docs.

report.summary: VoltAgent launched a curated directory of official MCP servers, filtering out unofficial forks and abandoned projects so AI assistants connect only to trusted, vendor-backed tools.
report.background: Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol in late 2024 as an open standard for connecting AI assistants to external tools and data. Adoption accelerated sharply through 2025 as OpenAI, Google and major IDE vendors like Cursor added MCP client support, and hundreds of servers appeared almost overnight. That speed created a trust problem: an MCP server can read private data and take real actions such as deploying code, sending email or mutating production databases, yet many community servers are forks, unmaintained, or published by anonymous authors. Supply-chain risk, prompt injection and credential exposure became mainstream concerns, and security researchers demonstrated malicious servers exfiltrating data. The new directory positions itself as a trust layer, listing only servers published by the company behind the product or by widely used open-source projects, and linking official vendor documentation where no public repository exists.
key_points: Trust as the core feature: every entry is either an official server from the company behind the product or a widely used open-source project. Unofficial forks and abandoned repositories are excluded, and where no public repo exists the directory links straight to the vendor's official MCP documentation instead.

Breadth across the stack: coverage spans cloud and hosting (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, Tencent, Alibaba), databases and analytics (Postgres, MongoDB, Snowflake, ClickHouse, BigQuery, DuckDB, Redis, Qdrant, Neo4j), CI/CD (CircleCI, Buildkite, GitLab, Harness) and observability (Datadog, Sentry, Grafana, PagerDuty, Langfuse).

Databases are the biggest category, with dozens of vendors including Neon, Supabase, PlanetScale, Prisma, MotherDuck, SingleStore, Couchbase, Milvus, Pinecone, Elasticsearch and Google's MCP Toolbox for Databases, signalling that agents querying live data is the fastest-growing MCP use case.

Monitoring, analytics and browser automation round out the list: Datadog, PostHog, Mixpanel, Amplitude, Netdata and Arize Phoenix sit alongside Scrapeless, Bright Data, Hyperbrowser, Browserbase, Skyvern and Mozilla's Firefox DevTools server, covering both observability and computer-use agents.

Several entries are marked as available through Claude connectors rather than public repos, including Vercel, Supabase, Airtable, MongoDB, Snowflake and Datadog, showing vendors increasingly ship MCP as a distribution channel embedded in assistants rather than as standalone developer tooling.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals a shift from protocol novelty to infrastructure consolidation: curated registries, vendor-official servers and gateway tools are becoming the de facto app store for agent capabilities, and vendors now treat MCP support as a growth channel rather than a side project. For developers, the directory removes much of the vetting burden when choosing integrations, but it does not eliminate risk — an official server still runs with the credentials you grant it, so sandboxing, scoped tokens and audit logging remain essential. For regular users, assistants like Claude, ChatGPT and Cursor quietly become dramatically more capable, able to deploy sites, query databases and debug incidents; the trade-off is that trust now rests on vendor identity rather than code review, making provenance and permissions the new user-facing concern.
report.tools: If you want to explore MCP hands-on, start with the Model Context Protocol spec and reference SDKs, then Anthropic's MCP Inspector for debugging servers locally. Docker MCP Toolkit provides a sandboxed gateway for running servers in containers, and Google's MCP Toolbox for Databases connects agents to SQL and NoSQL stores. Useful references include the VoltAgent official-mcp-servers list, awesome-mcp-servers for community projects, and mcp-grafana or mcp-neo4j as readable open-source server implementations to learn from.
